amendments.rule: Where the ASV's recasting leaves a preposition with no English word — the impersonal `קרא לְ` + suffix rendered as a personal passive, `וְקֹרָא לָךְ` → *and thou shalt be called*, or a dative `לְ` + suffix rendered as a bare English indirect object, `תְּנָה לִּי` → *give me* — the preposition is its own `unrepresented` unit and its suffix takes the English pronoun that realizes it, including a subject pronoun. This is rule 21's recasting clause outside the resultative `הָיָה לְ`, and it is the case where rule 18's *possessive or object* is not the whole range. **The `לְ` is the commonest case, not the condition.** The same recasting silences any preposition it leaves nothing to say: `צוּר עַל` → *besieged Tirzah* and `צִוִּיתִי עָלֶיךָ` → *commanded thee* leave `עַל` bare, `אֶל` goes the same way before a bare English object, and a `בְּ` whose object the ASV promotes to a direct object — *blew the trumpet* — keeps nothing either. Read the condition, not the lemma: ask whether the ASV spends an English word on what that preposition contributes. **And a word the ASV writes as part of a neighbouring morpheme's own compound rendering is not a word spent on the preposition.** Where a Hebrew adverb or noun standing beside the preposition is rendered by an English expression written in two or three words, that expression belongs whole to the morpheme it renders, exactly as rule 30 reads its one-English-word condition as one rendering rather than one token, and the preposition takes a word only where the ASV has written one for its own relation. `הֶחָצֵר סָבִיב לַמִּשְׁכָּן` → *the court round about the tabernacle* gives *round about* whole to `סָבִיב`, headed on *round* under rule 24, and leaves the `לְ` `unrepresented`, exactly as the coordinated `וְלַמִּזְבֵּחַ` beside it is left. Do not divide such an expression to give a present preposition something to hold: rule 11 gives each morpheme the English it licenses, and half of another morpheme's fixed rendering is not English this one licenses. Test by subtraction as elsewhere — drop the word and ask whether the preposition's own relation has gone unstated, or whether only the neighbouring expression has been broken in two. The corpus renders `סָבִיב` by *round about* headed on *round* in 144 units and by a bare *round* in two, one of them hedged and the other a doubled adverb for which the ASV writes a separate word for each occurrence, and it reads the whole compound as the adverb's own in four of the five units where a determined preposition follows it. **But read whether the preposition's own object is rendered at all before silencing it.** Every case above is one where the ASV writes English for what the preposition governs and leaves only the relation unstated — *besieged Tirzah*, *commanded thee*, *blew the trumpet*, *give me*, *round about the tabernacle*. Where instead the governed noun is itself left with no English of its own, and a single English word carries the predicate, the preposition and that noun together, rule 30's one-rendering condition is met and this rule does not reach it: the contiguous morphemes share one unit headed on the one carrying the lexeme, rather than one rendered morpheme standing beside others marked `unrepresented`, which is what rule 30 forbids for a fixed expression and what rule 22 forbids for a morpheme whose sense the ASV has written inside a fused word. `אִם־רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ` → *if it displease thee* gives *it displease* to `רַע`, `בְּ` and `עַיִן` in one unit headed on the verb, while the suffix keeps the *thee* written for it under rule 18, exactly as `הֵשִׁיב פָּנִים` → *deny* fuses under rule 30. **And the single English word need not carry a predicate, nor its noun be a construct.** Where a preposition stands on an absolute noun and the ASV recasts the whole phrase as one English adverb — `בֶּאֱמֶת` → *faithfully*, `בְּאָחוֹר` → *back* — no word is written for the preposition apart from the noun or for the noun apart from the preposition, so rule 30's condition is met on the same terms and the two share one unit headed on the noun, which carries the lexeme. Do not mark the preposition `unrepresented` on the ground that the one English word is the noun's ordinary rendering: what tells this case from the ones above is that a single English word stands for the pair, and the subtraction test below finds the noun's own rendering gone with it. Contiguity is rule 30's condition and it is the limit here too: `גָּדַל ... מִן` → *exceeded*, where the subject or the object stands between, is split by rule 2 and its preposition is `unrepresented` as before. Test by subtraction — drop the English word and ask whether the preposition's noun as well as its relation has gone unsaid; where the noun keeps a word of its own, this rule governs and the preposition is `unrepresented`. **And where the ASV writes no pronoun for the suffix either, that suffix is its own `unrepresented` unit beside its preposition.** This rule's first sentence places a pronoun the ASV has written; a reflexive or ethical dative the ASV renders by nothing at all — `קוּמִי לָךְ` → *Rise up*, `וּלְכִי־לָךְ` → *and come away*, `הָלַךְ לוֹ` → *is over and gone* — leaves neither morpheme an English word, and each goes `unrepresented` on its own merits under rule 11. Do not read a phrasal particle standing beside the verb as the dative's rendering: *up*, *away* and *forth* are the English verb's own under rule 44, and the subtraction test rules 16 and 43 use finds the verb's rendering diminished when they are dropped while the dative's relation is left unstated either way. Read what the ASV writes rather than the lemma, since the same construction is rendered both ways: where a pronoun is written for the suffix — `לֶךְ־לְךָ` → *Get thee out* — this rule's first sentence governs as before and the suffix takes it. **And the case of that pronoun is no part of the condition.** Rule 18 gives a suffix whatever English pronoun realizes it, a possessive as readily as an object one, so a dative, benefactive or reflexive `לְ` whose relation the ASV leaves unstated is `unrepresented` whichever the ASV writes: `יַגִּיד לוֹ` → *tell* ***him*** and `נָתַן לוֹ` → *given* ***him*** leave the preposition nothing, and so do `לְרַע לוֹ` → *to* ***his*** *hurt* and `מַאֲרִיךְ לוֹ` → *prolong* ***his*** *days*, where the ASV recasts the dative as a possessive determiner on the noun standing beside it. Do not fuse such a pair under rule 30 on the ground that a possessive states the belonging the preposition carries: the subtraction test this rule already runs finds that *his* is the very word a bare suffix takes in any possessive context, so no English word is spent on the preposition's own relation, and a noun the ASV supplies for that possessive to stand on is `added` under rule 20 as before. Rule 49's fused genitive is the other case and its own closing sentence marks the boundary: there the possessive marker is written on a word that would otherwise stand bare — `לַיהוָה` → *is Jehovah's* — and the `לְ` is itself the verbless clause's predicate, whereas an adjunct dative hanging on a finite verb or a participle is this rule's.

Rule 40 already sends the one-word case to rule 30, but its carve-out is stated only for a word that carries a predicate as well (`רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ` → *it displease thee*) and its illustrations of fusion elsewhere in the contract are all prepositions on construct nouns, so a verse pass could read either the predicate or the construct as the condition. The added sentences state the scope the rule's own subtraction test already implies and name the two shapes this chapter met; nothing in the corpus tables shown contradicts it, and the neighbouring fusions in rule 30 (`בְּתוֹךְ` → *among*, `כְּפִי` → *as*) are the same reasoning.

conventions: אִישׁ in construct on a following noun is decided by what the ASV writes for the pair, and this chapter writes all three shapes. One English word fuses the two morphemes under rule 30, headed on the morpheme carrying the lexeme: אַנְשֵׁי לָצוֹן → *Scoffers* (29.8), אַנְשֵׁי דָמִים → *The bloodthirsty* (29.10), אִישׁ תְּכָכִים → *the oppressor* (29.13). Two content words split under rule 28's attributive rendering, אִישׁ taking the generic noun with its determiner and the rectum the attributive: אִישׁ אַף → *An angry man* (29.22), אִישׁ עָוֶל → *An unjust man* (29.27). A relative clause puts the whole recasting on the rectum under rule 19, אִישׁ keeping only the substantival pronoun: אִישׁ תְּרוּמוֹת → *he* + *that exacteth gifts* (29.4), אִישׁ תּוֹכָחוֹת → *He* + *being often reproved* (29.1). Where אִישׁ is instead absolute before an attributive participle it takes its own word and the participle keeps the verb: אִישׁ אֹהֵב → *Whoso* + *loveth* (29.3).

An articleless attributive participle that the ASV recasts as a relative clause keeps the supplied *that* under rule 41 even where the ASV interposes another morpheme's rendering between the relative and the verb, and the unit is discontinuous under rule 25 rather than broken: מַחֲלִיק → *that flattereth* (29.5), אָץ → *that is hasty* (29.20), שׁוֹפֵט → *that ... judgeth* around *faithfully* (29.14), מַקְשֶׁה → *that ... hardeneth* around *being often reproved* (29.1). Do not hand such a relative to the construct noun's rectum standing between them: what licenses the word is the clause whose finite verb the participle renders. The rectum takes the relative only where no attributive participle stands in the phrase for it, which is what 29.4 is.

report: Read all 27 verses end to end against the candidate table. Two genuine cross-verse splits found; the rest of the table is the ASV rendering one word differently in different contexts, which the source licenses.

SPLIT 1 — the supplied relative of an articleless attributive participle. PRO.29.5 (מַחֲלִיק → *that flattereth*), PRO.29.14 (שׁוֹפֵט → *that ... judgeth*, discontinuous around *faithfully*) and PRO.29.20 (אָץ → *that is hasty*) all keep the supplied *that* with the participle under rule 41. PRO.29.1 gave the same *that* to the construct's rectum, leaving מַקְשֶׁה only *hardeneth*. The English relative clause there is *that ... hardeneth his neck*, whose finite verb is the participle's rendering, while the rectum's *being often reproved* is a non-finite adjunct licensing no relative. PRO.29.1 is patched to match PRO.29.14 exactly: *that* + *hardeneth* on מַקְשֶׁה, discontinuous around *being often reproved*, which stays with תּוֹכָחוֹת headed on *reproved*. PRO.29.4 is untouched — no participle stands there, so the relative goes with the rectum's recasting under rule 19 as before.

SPLIT 2 — a preposition on an absolute noun rendered by one English word. PRO.29.14 fuses בֶּאֱמֶת → *faithfully* under rule 30, headed on the noun; PRO.29.11 left בְּ `unrepresented` beside אָחוֹר → *back*, the same shape with the same one-word rendering. Rule 40's own subtraction test decides it — drop *back* and the noun's rendering goes with the relation, because only one English word stands for the pair — and rule 40's closing paragraph then hands the case to rule 30. PRO.29.11 is patched to one aligned unit on בְּ+אָחוֹר headed on אָחוֹר. That also brings the verse into line with the chapter's four other one-word fusions (29.8 *Scoffers*, 29.10 *bloodthirsty*, 29.12 *falsehood*, 29.13 *oppressor*).

Checked and found licensed, not split: all 27 waws (each difference is a connective the ASV wrote or did not write, counted clause by clause under rule 14, including the *Whether ... or* pair of 29.9 where the Hebrew writes a connective for each member); the four אַיִן units, each headed on its negation word under rule 50 with only the ASV's own frame differing; עַל unrepresented in 29.5 beside עַל → *to* in 29.12 and *for* in 29.5b, which is rule 40 against a written word; the twelve light-verb units, all headed on the complement under rule 44, against the three phrasal particles (*turn away*, *stirreth up*, *meet together*), all headed on the verb; the eleven substantival adjectives, all taking their supplied determiner under rule 46 and heading on the lexeme word; and the seven אִישׁ-construct phrases, decided three ways by what the ASV writes rather than by the construction.

Copula placement is consistent across the chapter: 29.6 and 29.20 put the presentative frame on the nominal predicate with the prepositional phrase a modifier (rule 49's closing paragraph), while 29.26 puts *cometh* on the מִן that is itself the predicate. 29.27, 29.12, 29.18, 29.23, 29.24 and 29.10 all put a supplied copula on the predicate morpheme under rule 20.

BSB: none of the five disagreements is an error. עַל in 29.5 and the waws in 29.9, 29.19 and 29.21 are places where the ASV writes no English at all (rules 40 and 14) — the documented convention difference. בְּ in 29.11 is now represented as part of the fused *back* unit, but the patch rests on the chapter's own rule-30 practice and rule 40's subtraction test, not on the comparison.

One amendment returned: rule 40's one-word carve-out is written around a single English word that carries a predicate (`רַע בְּעֵינֶיךָ` → *it displease thee*), and PRO.29.11 and PRO.29.14 are the same carve-out with no predicate in the word. The replacement text says so in that rule rather than leaving the narrow example to be read as the condition.
